title: The seal
hookLine: a priest may never reveal what he hears, under any pressure (CCC 1467)
tomorrow: The tabernacle and the red lamp

cards: Everyone knows what it's like to tell a secret and watch it travel. You tell one friend, and within a week three people look at you differently.

So why would anyone walk into a small room and tell a stranger the worst things they've done? Part of the answer is a promise the Catholic Church makes, one of the strictest promises of silence in the world.
The priest who hears you will carry it to his grave.

teach.h: SIGILLUM: A SEAL ON A LETTER.
teach.b: It's called a seal because it's meant to stay closed like a sealed letter, the old kind with wax and a signet ring, never to be opened. The Latin word is sigillum.
The Catechism, in paragraph 1467, says a priest who hears confessions is bound to absolute secrecy about the sins confessed to him, with no exceptions. Church law calls the seal inviolable.
A priest may not reveal a penitent's sins by word, by hint, or in any other way, to anyone, ever.
Not to the police, not to a court, not to the penitent's family, not even to the penitent later, unless the penitent brings it up. He can't even use what he heard to change how he treats someone.
A priest who directly breaks the seal is automatically excommunicated. And it binds others too: an interpreter, or anyone who overhears. Why so strict?
Because the whole sacrament depends on it.
If people couldn't trust the silence, they wouldn't come, and the door to forgiveness would close.
Catholics tell the story of John of Nepomuk, a priest in Prague, drowned in the river in 1393 on the orders of King Wenceslaus the Fourth.
Tradition says the king wanted to know what his queen had confessed, and John refused. Historians debate the details, but he's honored as a martyr of the seal.
In our own time, some governments have tried to require priests to report certain things heard in confession.
The Church's answer hasn't changed: the seal can't be broken. That doesn't mean a priest does nothing. He can urge a penitent to turn themselves in or to get help.

how: Catholics confess trusting that the priest is bound by the seal: he may never reveal or use what he hears, and a priest who directly breaks it is automatically excommunicated.

games.q: you're John of Nepomuk. the king demands to know what the queen said in confession. what do you do?
o: tell him, since he's the king.
hint at it without saying it outright.
games.why: tradition says he refused and was drowned in Prague's river in 1393. historians debate the details, but he's honored as a martyr of the seal.

practice: Think of something someone told you in confidence, a worry, a mistake, a hope they aren't ready to share, and picture their face, and the trust in it, as they told you.
Quietly decide it stays with you: not a hint, not a knowing look, not a someone told me. If you pray, pray for that person without naming what they said.

wordCard.voice: Sigillum. Latin for seal, the absolute silence a priest keeps about what he hears, with no exceptions, so that anyone can come. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a seal, a small sign pressed into wax. Church law calls the seal of confession sigillum sacramentale.

carryVoice: Your line: what's said there stays there. That's confession, up close: conscience, walking in, contrition, absolution, the seal. Tomorrow, a red lamp in the dark.
